title: The One With The Lesbian Wedding

jokes.text: Ross announcing Carol and Susan are getting married, followed by his visible discomfort and finger getting stuck in the chair
jokes.setup: Carol announces she and Susan are getting married, putting Ross in an awkward position as Carol's ex-husband
jokes.punchline: Ross tries to be gracious about it, fails to mask his discomfort, and literally gets his finger stuck in the chair — a physical manifestation of his emotional trap
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of the finger stuck in the chair is a perfect visual metaphor for Ross's emotional state — he's trapped. The character integration is excellent; only Ross in this specific situation could deliver this layered moment of verbal gracious-ness vs. physical betrayal.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, the baby started it!

jokes.text: "As in, 'I now pronounce you wife and wife' married?"
jokes.setup: Carol tells Ross she and Susan are getting married
jokes.punchline: Ross repeats back the concept in his own words, emphasizing the strangeness of it to him with mock-ceremonial phrasing
jokes.explanation: A competent line that captures Ross's stunned processing. The phrasing 'wife and wife' is functional but not particularly inventive — it does what it needs to do without being remarkable.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Ross, there's something I need to tell you. It's about us.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: I'm a lesbian.

jokes.text: "Why wouldn't I want to come? I had fun at the first wedding."
jokes.setup: Carol says she understands if Ross doesn't want to come to the wedding
jokes.punchline: Ross references having attended the first Carol/Susan ceremony (from the pilot), implying it was fine — but the absurdity of 'I had fun' at the wedding to the woman who left him for another woman is the real joke
jokes.explanation: Strong character-specific line with excellent economy. The callback to the pilot rewards long-time viewers. Only Ross could say this; the deadpan delivery of 'I had fun' about such a loaded event is genuinely funny and characterful.

jokes.text: Ross trying to be gracious about the wedding while his finger is stuck in the chair: 'I'm reveling, baby. Believe me. Is your finger caught in that chair?'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to convince Carol he's happy for her while clearly not being so
jokes.punchline: Carol notices Ross's finger is stuck in the chair, fully exposing his physical discomfort as a mirror of his emotional state
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff to the physical setup established a moment before. The juxtaposition of Ross's verbal magnanimity ('I'm reveling, baby') with his literal physical entrapment is beautifully structured. The line 'Is your finger caught in that chair?' as a quiet, concerned question rather than a punchline makes it funnier. Excellent cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh sure, I'd love to go to your wedding. It'll be just like my wedding to Carol, except this time I won't have to pay for it.

jokes.text: Joey watching himself on TV: 'I'm on Days of our Lives.' Then: 'Then I started thinking about us, and how these are the days of our lives.'
jokes.setup: Joey watching his soap opera appearance on TV, getting emotional about his life
jokes.punchline: He pivots to a philosophical musing using the show's title as a literal statement about life — oblivious to how cheesy it is
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey moment — his sincerity makes the terrible pun funny. He's not making a pun intentionally, he genuinely means it, which is the joke. Good character integration but the wordplay itself is groan-level.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm reveling, baby! I'm reveling!

jokes.text: Monica and Rachel celebrating when they hear Carol and Susan's caterer had a bike accident and is in a full-body cast — shouting 'Yes!' in unison
jokes.setup: Monica explains the caterer had an accident and is in a full-body cast
jokes.punchline: Monica and Rachel shout 'Yes!' in unison at news of someone's injury because it means Monica can cater the wedding
jokes.explanation: The unison 'Yes!' at someone's misfortune is a sharp, dark comedic beat that works because of how unselfconscious it is. Monica's competitive/ambitious nature is perfectly captured. Good economy — the joke is entirely in the reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm so happy for you guys, really. This is great.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Thanks, Ross. That means a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, seriously, I'm thrilled. You two are perfect together.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Um, guys? You can go now. You should probably leave.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: What? We just got here.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know, but I'm kind of... stuck. Behind this couch. So if you could just...

jokes.text: Chandler singing: 'Who's the bitterest man in the living room? The bitterest man in the living room?'
jokes.setup: Joey says Carol and Susan love each other and want to celebrate with people close to them, implying Ross should attend
jokes.punchline: Chandler breaks into a mocking little song about Ross's bitterness rather than engaging with the conversation earnestly
jokes.explanation: Very Chandler — deflecting with irony and a musical jab. The specificity of the improvised song and its cheerful melody against bitter content is characteristic. High quotability because it's the kind of thing people repeat. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's not just a job, it's my life. Days of Our Lives.

jokes.text: "If she were marrying a guy, she'd be the worst lesbian ever."
jokes.setup: Ross argues 'If she were marrying a guy, you wouldn't expect me to go'
jokes.punchline: Chandler points out the logical absurdity — Carol marrying a man would contradict her entire identity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Perfect logical structure — it takes Ross's faulty hypothetical and demolishes it with precise, compressed wit. The economy is exceptional (one sentence, complete joke). 'The worst lesbian ever' is a memorable, quotable phrase. This is Chandler at his most effective: weaponizing logic for comedy. Justifiably scores 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's terrible!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, so terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: When is the wedding?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Saturday.

jokes.text: Phoebe asking 'Did I miss it?' about Joey's TV appearance; Joey: 'No, I'm on right after this guy shoots himself.'
jokes.setup: They're all gathered to watch Joey's first appearance on Days of Our Lives
jokes.punchline: Joey casually references a character shooting himself as a scheduling marker, with zero emotional weight
jokes.explanation: A nice casual dark-comedy beat. Joey's breezy delivery about the shooting makes it funny. Not a landmark joke but competently executed.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: But why do they even need to get married? I mean, they're happy together.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ross. Because they're in love? Hello?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, but that's not really a reason...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's not a reason? What else do you need, a coupon?

jokes.text: Joey talking about the actress: 'She's really nice. She taught me about how to work with the cameras and smell-the-fart acting.'
jokes.setup: Joey mentions a pretty actress who was helpful on set
jokes.punchline: He introduces the term 'smell-the-fart acting' — a hilariously lowbrow name for a real soap opera technique
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout moments and a culturally memorable Friends joke. 'Smell-the-fart acting' is an inspired phrase that perfectly satirizes soap opera acting while being exactly the kind of term Joey would learn and earnestly repeat. The phrase is so specific, so vivid, and so perfectly calibrated to Joey's character that it has entered pop culture. Justifies 8+ easily — it's a genuinely great comic invention.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: ♪ Ross is bitter, Ross is sad, Ross's love life's really bad, he's bitter, so bitter, Ross the bitter guy ♪

jokes.text: Joey demonstrating 'smell-the-fart acting' on camera — holding a long dramatic pause with an intense constipated expression
jokes.setup: Joey has explained smell-the-fart acting and is now demonstrating it live
jokes.punchline: The physical performance itself — Joey's exaggerated, clearly ridiculous soap opera face held for an uncomfortably long beat
jokes.explanation: The visual payoff to the 'smell-the-fart' setup. Matt LeBlanc's physical commitment to the bit makes this land as hard as the verbal joke. The extended hold on the face is the key — it's funny for longer than it should be. Earns 8+ as a physical callback with strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, Carol IS marrying a guy. She's marrying Susan's girlfriend.

jokes.text: Joey on TV doing smell-the-fart acting for a full 8 seconds before saying 'subcranial hematoma'
jokes.setup: Joey's scene as Dr. Drake Ramoray begins with a dramatic pause
jokes.punchline: The audience now recognizes the technique in real time — Joey is doing the smell-the-fart face on national television, followed by an overwrought medical term
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the setup AND demonstration — seeing the technique deployed in its natural habitat on an actual soap opera, with the group watching live. The structural escalation is excellent: explain → demonstrate → see in context. 'Subcranial hematoma' is the perfect pompous medical gibberish for this moment. The subsequent 'perhaps we can discuss this further over coffee' makes it even funnier as a non-sequitur. High impact in a group viewing context.

jokes.text: Joey's Dr. Drake Ramoray after delivering dire medical news: 'Perhaps we can discuss this further over coffee.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Drake Ramoray has just gravely informed a woman her sister has a subcranial hematoma
jokes.punchline: He pivots immediately to asking her for coffee — wildly inappropriate but delivered with soap opera smoothness
jokes.explanation: Sharp absurdist beat satirizing soap opera doctor characters who are simultaneously medical experts and serial romantic leads. The tonal whiplash from 'dire hematoma' to 'coffee?' is perfectly executed and Joey's earnestness sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So this actress, she taught me about sfumato. It's like, you know, when you're acting and you gotta blend all your emotions together, make it all smoky and mysterious.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I've been doing it wrong the whole time. I thought it was 'sfu-mah-toe.' Turns out it's 'sfoo-mah-toe.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No wait, that's not even a real acting thing, is it?

jokes.text: Chandler's review: 'Nice! For a minute, I thought you were actually smelling something.'
jokes.setup: Everyone has just watched Joey's dramatic pause performance on TV
jokes.punchline: Chandler's backhanded compliment references the smell-the-fart acting terminology, calling it convincing while also being gently brutal
jokes.explanation: Chandler's callback to the smell-the-fart gag lands as a well-timed button on the whole sequence. The faint praise structure ('Nice! For a minute...') is perfectly Chandler. Adds rewatch value as the closing punctuation to the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's a very important acting technique. You smell the fart.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You smell the fart?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, you know, like this...

jokes.text: Ross: 'I gotta get to work. I got a big dinosaur bone to inspect.' Chandler: 'No, that's me.'
jokes.setup: Ross says he has a 'big dinosaur bone to inspect' as he leaves
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately claims the double entendre as referring to himself
jokes.explanation: A fairly standard innuendo joke. The structure works and Chandler's delivery would sell it, but the comedic concept is well-worn. Gets a solid laugh in the room but isn't inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm afraid I have some very serious news about your condition.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But first, has anyone ever told you that you have the most beautiful eyes I've ever seen? Are you a patient here too, or are you just naturally this gorgeous?

jokes.text: Phoebe tells Monica a client died on her massage table; Monica: 'That's a little more relaxed than you want them to get.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe announces a client died on the massage table today
jokes.punchline: Monica responds with a clinical, massage-world-appropriate understatement about over-relaxation
jokes.explanation: A well-crafted dark comedy line with excellent economy. The reframing of death as 'too relaxed' in the massage context is cleverly absurd and Monica's matter-of-fact delivery makes it land. Strong punchline for a dark premise.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What is that? What are you doing with your face?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm doing the smell-the-fart acting.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, it looks like you're straining to pass one.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'She probably woke up this morning and thought I'll have some breakfast, take a walk, then have my massage. Little did she know God thought, "Okay, but that's it."'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is processing the death of her 82-year-old client and imagining what the woman's morning was like
jokes.punchline: God's imagined response — 'Okay, but that's it' — as a casual divine sign-off on a life, delivered in Phoebe's warm, earnest tone
jokes.explanation: A lovely Phoebe joke — the casual anthropomorphization of God as someone who just lets you have your last nice morning before pulling the plug is both sweet and darkly funny. The phrase 'Okay, but that's it' as divine bureaucratic sign-off is inspired. High character integration; this is pure Phoebe cosmology.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's what she said.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, no. It's a dinosaur bone. I have to inspect it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I know.

jokes.text: Monica deliberating over wedding food: 'I can't decide between lamb or duck.' Joey: 'Well, lambs are scarier. Or the movie would've been called Silence of the Ducks.'
jokes.setup: Monica can't decide between lamb and duck for the wedding menu
jokes.punchline: Joey applies a completely irrelevant horror movie logic to distinguish the meats, missing the point entirely
jokes.explanation: Excellent Joey joke. The logic is absurd but internally consistent — he's genuinely trying to help using the only framework that occurred to him. 'Silence of the Ducks' is a funny, specific image. High character integration and quotability. The gap between what was asked and what was answered is the engine of the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm okay. It's just my client Mrs. Adelman died.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, she fell down the stairs. But the good news is I charged her for the massage anyway because I'd already lit the scented candles.

jokes.text: Rachel describing her coffee order: 'I had the half-drunk cappuccino with the lipstick on the rim. And this with the cigarette butt in it, is that decaf?'
jokes.setup: Waitress asks who ordered what among Rachel's messy table
jokes.punchline: Rachel's identifiers for her drinks are hilariously specific and gross — the lipstick rim, the cigarette butt — indicating the cafe is a disaster
jokes.explanation: A solid observational gag about the chaos of Central Perk, though this seems to be a different setting given the mess. The specificity of the identifiers (lipstick, cigarette butt) is good comic detail. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, at least they died doing what they loved... relaxing.

jokes.text: Mrs. Adelman (voiced through Phoebe): 'Talk about crap, just listen to Stella Neidman tell her story about Rod Steiger for the hundredth time.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is worried about her mom thinking her life is 'crap' since she didn't marry Barry; Phoebe suddenly channels Mrs. Adelman
jokes.punchline: The dead woman's spirit interrupts with a completely irrelevant complaint about another old woman's boring story, in a totally different voice
jokes.explanation: The first full deployment of the Mrs. Adelman possession gag and it's funny because of the specificity — she complains about someone named 'Stella Neidman' and Rod Steiger, very specific dead-lady grievances. The absurdist left-turn from Rachel's genuine anxiety is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: She probably woke up this morning, looked at her calendar and said, 'Well, I'm gonna have a nice breakfast, maybe take a walk in the park... and then I'm gonna die.'

jokes.text: Mrs. Adelman/Phoebe suddenly snapping 'Sit up!' in the middle of a conversation
jokes.setup: Ross asks how long the dead woman's spirit will be with them
jokes.punchline: Rather than answering that question, Mrs. Adelman takes over and barks 'Sit up!' — the imperious behavior of an old woman asserting herself even in death
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — two words and a complete character portrait. 'Sit up!' is funny because it's so specific, bossy, and disconnected from what anyone was discussing. The interruption timing is good.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So it's lamb or duck for the catering?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, you know what they say... 'Silence of the Ducks.'

jokes.text: Sandra to Monica: 'The last time I saw you, it was eat or be eaten.'
jokes.setup: Rachel introduces Monica to her mother
jokes.punchline: Sandra's casual reference to Monica's past weight — framed as a survival-of-the-fittest situation — is a shockingly blunt crack delivered with cheerful warmth
jokes.explanation: A sharp line that establishes Sandra as casually cruel without realizing it. The animalistic framing ('eat or be eaten') is memorably specific and mean. The economy is strong. Slightly cheap in that it relies on fat-shaming but the character specificity elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, so this one has a mysterious brown film, hints of what I'm hoping is just coffee, with a finish of—is that a thumbprint?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And this beauty here features a lovely crusty rim, notes of old lipstick, and what appears to be a fossilized food particle from the Clinton administration.

jokes.text: Sandra dismissing Rachel's job: 'If you didn't pour the coffee, no one would have anything to drink. Believe me, sometimes that happens.'
jokes.setup: Sandra is supposedly praising Rachel for her 'big job'
jokes.punchline: The praise collapses into a frank admission that pouring coffee is the whole job, with the kicker 'Believe me, sometimes that happens' implying this is a low bar
jokes.explanation: Competent character work for Sandra — her backhanded compliments reveal the mother-daughter dynamic economically. 'Believe me, sometimes that happens' as a kicker is good. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: My stories! Where are my stories? It's 2 o'clock, my stories come on at 2 o'clock!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And why is everything so bright? Turn down the lights! My eyes! My poor old eyes!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And who keeps eating my prune juice? I bought prune juice!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Also, my bosom itches.

jokes.text: Mrs. Adelman/Phoebe interrupts with: 'I know who you remind me of. Evelyn Durmer. That's before the lousy face-lift. Now she looks like Soupy Sales.'
jokes.setup: Sandra is having a touching moment expressing pride in Rachel
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Adelman bursts in with an unsolicited comparison involving an unflattering face-lift and a reference to Soupy Sales (an obscure comedian) that no one in the room would understand
jokes.explanation: Good iteration of the Mrs. Adelman gag. The specificity of 'Soupy Sales' as the comparison point for a face-lift gone wrong is funny precisely because it's such a specific, dated reference. It perfectly characterizes this dead old woman.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm sensing a woman... she's very old... she's telling me something...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: She says... 'GET OUT OF MY APARTMENT!'

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Who's Evelyn Durmer?' Rachel: 'I don't know. Who's Soupy Sales?'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Adelman has just compared someone to Evelyn Durmer post-Soupy Sales face-lift
jokes.punchline: Both women are confused by different parts of the reference — neither can decode Mrs. Adelman's world
jokes.explanation: A neat button on the previous joke — the parallel confusion of both characters about different parts of the same reference is structurally clean. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra Green
dialogue.line: I mean, what is this place? Is it a coffee shop? A furniture store? I can't even tell.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, Mom, it's called 'eclectic.' It's very fun not knowing what anything is.

jokes.text: Sandra: 'There's an unattractive nude man playing the cello.'
jokes.setup: Sandra is looking around at the eclectic life Rachel has built
jokes.punchline: Casual, matter-of-fact description of a nude cellist as if this is merely slightly notable
jokes.explanation: A great visual-comedy line. The specificity ('unattractive') and the bureaucratic matter-of-factness of the observation makes it funnier than a simple 'there's a nude man.' Sandra's deadpan delivery concept is well-captured in the writing.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: Hey Monica, you look great!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Thanks!

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: I mean, after everything you went through... it's like you came back from the brink of darkness itself.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Just be glad he's not playing a smaller instrument.'
jokes.setup: Sandra has just observed an unattractive nude man playing the cello
jokes.punchline: Chandler implies that a smaller instrument would mean less coverage — an innuendo about nudity and visibility
jokes.explanation: A reliable Chandler innuendo. Well-timed response to Sandra's observation. The logic is sound and clever even if the underlying joke is fairly standard. Chandler's role as the quip-machine is well-served.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: You know, being a waitress is a really important job. You're providing a service, you're part of the hospitality industry.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, yesterday I forgot to bring someone their food.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: Oh, that happens.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: They were still waiting when I left.

jokes.text: Sandra reveals she's considering leaving Rachel's father — immediately after saying 'I look at you and I think this is what I want. For me.'
jokes.setup: Sandra is praising Rachel's independent life and saying she's never seen her so happy
jokes.punchline: The warmth of 'I look at you and I think this is what I want' turns out to mean Sandra wants it for herself — she's leaving the father
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed misdirection that pivots a sweet mother-daughter moment into a bomb-drop. The slow-build of Sandra's praise before the reveal is structurally sound. The cringe of Rachel realizing her independence inspired her mom to leave her dad gives it emotional resonance alongside the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Adelman's Spirit
dialogue.line: Look at her face! She's had more work done than a highway construction site. And those lips! I've seen trout with smaller mouths.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Adelman's Spirit
dialogue.line: She's dressed like she's still going to Studio 54. Honey, that ended in 1986. So did your relevance.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Adelman's Spirit
dialogue.line: All that Botox and she still can't smile. She looks like she's perpetually smelling something bad.

jokes.text: Monica: 'All right, tell me if this is too cute. Lesbian wedding, chicken breasts.'
jokes.setup: Monica is planning the menu for Carol and Susan's wedding
jokes.punchline: She proposes 'chicken breasts' as a menu item at a lesbian wedding, completely oblivious to the double entendre, asking only if it's 'too cute'
jokes.explanation: A great Monica joke — she's so focused on the food that she entirely misses the obvious double entendre she's walking into. 'Tell me if this is too cute' before 'chicken breasts' at a lesbian wedding is wonderfully oblivious. Strong character integration (only Monica would be this single-mindedly food-focused) and good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: Oh my God, look at that guy playing cello in the window across the street. And he's completely naked!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what they say... the bigger the instrument, the smaller the—

jokes.text: Ross's reaction to the 'chicken breasts' suggestion: 'Oh God. I think I'm gonna be sick.' Monica: 'What? It's not like I'm putting little nipples on them.'
jokes.setup: Monica has just proposed 'chicken breasts' at the lesbian wedding
jokes.punchline: Monica's defense — 'It's not like I'm putting little nipples on them' — escalates the double entendre to an even more graphic level while she remains oblivious
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the already-funny chicken breasts joke to an even more inappropriate level via Monica's completely innocent defense is excellent. 'It's not like I'm putting little nipples on them' is one of the episode's most quotable lines. The escalation structure — making it worse while trying to make it better — is classic sitcom craft.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: Rachel, I just want to know... are you really happy?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Of course I am, Sandra. Why would you ask me that?

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: I don't know, you just seem like something's missing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, nothing's missing. I have my job, my friends, my apartment—

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: I'm getting married.

jokes.text: Mrs. Adelman/Phoebe: 'You know, in my day, divorce was not an option.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is reacting to the news that Sandra is leaving Rachel's dad
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Adelman weighs in with a casually judgmental old-fashioned opinion, inserted into a contemporary emotional crisis
jokes.explanation: A solid if predictable iteration of the Mrs. Adelman gag — the joke is that she keeps inserting dated opinions into modern situations. This one is more expected than the earlier Stella Neidman/Soupy Sales versions. Still functional.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Is a lesbian wedding with chicken breast too cute?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, it's perfect!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, the chicken breasts are so tender and juicy, and when you bite into them, the juices just run down your... I mean, it's really moist.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, why are you getting so defensive about chicken?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm not! I'm just saying the nipples— I mean, the peaks of flavor are really highlighted by the lemon glaze.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'When I was little, all parents got divorced. I figured as an adult I wouldn't have to worry about it.' Chandler: 'Can't you look at this as flattering? She just wants to be like you.' Rachel: 'Well, couldn't she have just copied my haircut?'
jokes.setup: Rachel is devastated that her mom is leaving her dad and wants to be like Rachel
jokes.punchline: Rachel wishes her mom had just copied her haircut instead of copying her independence — a very Rachel-specific response
jokes.explanation: The punchline is perfectly Rachel — someone who would rather her mom admire her hair than her life choices. It's both funny and a sharp character observation. Chandler's setup ('can't you look at this as flattering?') is perfectly calibrated to get the punchline response. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I mean, isn't there supposed to be some age where you stop worrying about your parents getting divorced? Like, I thought that was supposed to happen when I turned 18, or moved out, or got married...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: But apparently not. Apparently you worry about it forever.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'When my parents divorced, they sent me to a shrink and she told me that kids blame themselves. But in your case, it's actually kind of true.'
jokes.setup: Chandler offers advice about parental divorce based on his own experience
jokes.punchline: He undermines the therapeutic wisdom by noting that in Rachel's specific case — where her independence inspired her mom — the kid-blaming-themselves thing is literally accurate
jokes.explanation: A sharp, dark Chandler joke that subverts therapeutic wisdom with a situational truth. The structure is elegant — build up a comforting psychological fact, then twist it into an accusation. Chandler's delivery of dark truths with cheerful matter-of-factness is well-captured. Genuinely clever.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Look, it's not your fault. Parents always blame themselves for the divorce.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: But in your case, Rachel, you really should have seen the signs.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Damn. My mail-order grandfather hasn't come yet.' (when the doorbell rings and it's Mr. Adelman)
jokes.setup: The doorbell rings unexpectedly
jokes.punchline: Chandler's non-sequitur about waiting for a 'mail-order grandfather' — the idea of ordering elderly relatives via catalog delivered with complete straight-face conviction
jokes.explanation: A good Chandler non-sequitur. 'Mail-order grandfather' is an absurd concept delivered with his characteristic deflecting humor. It implies something sad about his own family situation while being funny. Good economy and originality.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I ordered a grandfather clock through the mail!

jokes.text: Mr. Adelman: 'That's okay. Although you did cut into my busy day of sitting.' Phoebe: 'Um, do you want to sit?' Mr. Adelman: 'No, I spent most of my morning trying to stand up.'
jokes.setup: Mr. Adelman arrives after being called; Phoebe offers him a seat
jokes.punchline: He declines to sit because he just spent the morning trying to stand up — his elderly physical reality delivered with perfect dry resignation
jokes.explanation: Lovely old-man comedy with perfect internal logic — of course he doesn't want to sit down; he just worked so hard to stand. The setup ('busy day of sitting') and the elaboration ('spent my morning trying to stand') work in lovely parallel. Strong character-specific writing for a one-scene guest.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Thank you so much for coming to meet with me, Mr. Adelman.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Adelman
dialogue.line: Well, I didn't have anything else to do. I'm 81 years old. My days are pretty much wide open.

jokes.text: Mr. Adelman, after hearing his dead wife's spirit is in Phoebe: 'I remember she also said she wanted to sleep with me one last time.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe asks if Mr. Adelman can think of any unfinished business his wife had that would make her spirit linger
jokes.punchline: After a genuine answer ('she wanted to see everything'), he adds that she wanted one last sexual encounter with him — a completely unexpected escalation from a sweet old man
jokes.explanation: A great subversive joke — the sweet old widower suddenly making a very direct proposition, but through the cover of his dead wife's supposed wishes. The pause before he adds it and the delivery ('Worth a shot, huh?') elevate this significantly. The misdirection of establishing him as sweet and genuine makes the pivot funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Adelman
dialogue.line: No thank you, I'm fine standing. My knees don't bend anymore.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'I'm sorry. There's laughing in my head.' (while trying to keep a straight face after Mr. Adelman's proposition)
jokes.setup: Mr. Adelman has just suggested his dead wife wanted to sleep with him one last time (through Phoebe)
jokes.punchline: Phoebe, trying to honor the situation, can only explain that Mrs. Adelman's spirit is laughing inside her — a polite way of saying this is ridiculous
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's explanation that 'there's laughing in my head' is a beautifully economical, character-specific way to react. It respects the absurd premise (she is genuinely channeling Mrs. Adelman) while acknowledging the comedy. The line is highly quotable and very Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Adelman
dialogue.line: Would you do me a favor? My wife, she's been dead for eight years. Would you sleep with me?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Adelman
dialogue.line: Okay, well, if you talk to her, tell her I said hello.

jokes.text: Mr. Adelman: 'Worth a shot, huh?' (after Phoebe indicates Mrs. Adelman's spirit is laughing at the proposition)
jokes.setup: Mr. Adelman has been gently rejected via Phoebe laughing as the spirit
jokes.punchline: 'Worth a shot, huh?' — a completely unruffled, dignified acknowledgment that he tried and failed
jokes.explanation: Three words that perfectly close the gag. 'Worth a shot, huh?' from a grieving elderly man who just tried to get a date via his wife's ghost is both funny and somehow touching. Perfect economy and character work for a guest role.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Look at Barry's costume!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What is he supposed to be?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A dentist.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What was he before?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A dentist.

jokes.text: Sandra looking at Halloween photos: 'Oh, and look, here's Barry. He came straight from the office?' 'Oh, no. That was his costume. See, he's actually an orthodontist, but he came as a regular dentist.'
jokes.setup: Sandra is looking at Halloween photos and sees Barry in what appears to be an office costume
jokes.punchline: Barry's Halloween costume was dressing as a regular dentist instead of his specialty (orthodontist) — a profoundly boring, deeply Barry-appropriate Halloween costume
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The concept — an orthodontist going as a regular dentist for Halloween — is genuinely original and says everything about Barry's dull personality without him being present. It's the perfect sitcom joke: specific, surprising, and instantly tells you everything about the character. The explanation 'he came as a regular dentist' delivered deadpan is exceptional. Justifies 8+ easily.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I said I don't need your help!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, what you said was, 'Get out of my apartment, you're useless and you're in my way.'

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, that's what I meant.

jokes.text: Monica admitting she planned extensively but 'just didn't plan enough time to do it'
jokes.setup: Everything is behind schedule; Monica insists she planned everything
jokes.punchline: The planning was perfect except for the time needed to actually execute the plan
jokes.explanation: A solid Monica character joke. Her compulsive planning running into reality is well-worn territory for the character, but the specific framing ('I planned and planned. I just didn't plan enough time to do it') is a good paradox. Competent.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm so excited for girls' time! We could go shopping, get manicures, maybe catch a movie?

dialogue.speaker: Sandra's Mother
dialogue.line: That sounds lovely, dear. Do you happen to know where I could score some cocaine?

jokes.text: Mrs. Adelman/Phoebe at the wedding prep gathering: 'Does anybody have any marijuana?'
jokes.setup: Phoebe/Mrs. Adelman is enjoying being 'just the girls' at the wedding prep
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Adelman, through Phoebe, asks if anyone has marijuana — a dead 82-year-old woman's bucket-list curiosity delivered casually
jokes.explanation: A great escalation of the Mrs. Adelman gag. The idea that a dead 82-year-old woman would use the opportunity of possessing Phoebe's body to finally try marijuana is both absurd and oddly poignant. The casual phrasing makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: So girls, I want to be modern and hip like you. Can I ask... how often do you have sex?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Um... that's... really personal.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, maybe we should talk about something else?

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm trying to be cool! Come on, just tell me!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: This is either the best or worst thing that's ever happened.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Look, no one's smoking pot around all this food.' Mrs. Adelman/Phoebe: 'Well, that's fine. I never did it. I just thought I might.'
jokes.setup: Monica refuses to allow marijuana at the food prep
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Adelman/Phoebe accepts the refusal with complete equanimity — she just wondered, no big deal
jokes.explanation: The button on the marijuana joke. Mrs. Adelman's shrug-it-off response ('I never did it. I just thought I might.') is perfectly calibrated — not desperate, just lightly curious. Good character consistency.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: Well, I've only been with one man... Rachel's father.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I'm gonna stop you right there. I don't need to hear this.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I really, really don't need to hear this.

jokes.text: Mrs. Adelman/Phoebe: 'What's new in sex?'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Adelman, possessing Phoebe, is bonding with the women at the wedding prep
jokes.punchline: She asks about sex with the candid directness of someone who is 82 and has nothing to lose — plus the implication she's been missing out
jokes.explanation: Brilliant in its economy — four words that are immediately funny. 'What's new in sex?' from a dead 82-year-old woman is a perfect question. The gap between the speaker's implied life experience and the casual framing of sex as a topical subject to catch up on is inspired. One of the episode's best lines.

dialogue.line: Parallel between Rachel not marrying Barry and Sandra regretting marrying hers

jokes.text: Sandra: 'The only man I've been with is your father.' Rachel: 'I'm dicing. I'm dicing. I don't hear anything.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Adelman has asked 'what's new in sex?' and Sandra takes it as an opening to discuss her own situation
jokes.punchline: Rachel furiously dices vegetables while declaring she can't hear her mother discussing her sex life
jokes.explanation: A reliable cringe-comedy reaction: child refusing to acknowledge parent's sexuality. Rachel's 'I'm dicing' as a coping mechanism is good physical comedy. Solid but standard.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, you're like a Nazi general planning a military campaign in here.

jokes.text: Monica in drill-sergeant mode: 'Move, move, move!' Rachel: 'I feel like you should have German subtitles.'
jokes.setup: Monica is running the kitchen like a military operation with 12 hours left
jokes.punchline: Rachel's observation that Monica's intensity evokes a German military film — a specific, visual reference to Monica's intensity
jokes.explanation: A nice observation that captures Monica's kitchen-army persona. The German subtitles image is specific and funny. Competent character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, come on, speed it up!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm trying, but these pigs in a blanket, they're not cooperating with me. Look at this one — he's just lying there, completely unresponsive.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: They're pigs in a blanket, Joey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know what they are, but he's not listening to me!

jokes.text: Joey: 'I'm sorry! It's the pigs! They're reluctant to get in the blanket!'
jokes.setup: Monica demands Joey speed up with the pigs-in-blanket
jokes.punchline: Joey treats the pigs-in-blanket as an actual standoff with reluctant pigs, speaking about them as if they have agency and opinions about blankets
jokes.explanation: A delightful Joey joke. The idea that the pigs are 'reluctant' and that Joey is sympathizing with their perspective on the blanketing process is perfect character comedy. Only Joey would apologize on behalf of resistant hors d'oeuvres. High quotability and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, if you don't help me with this wedding, I'm going to kill you. And it's not going to be quick. I'm going to take my time. I'm going to make it hurt. And then I'm going to serve you at the reception as pigs in a blanket.

jokes.text: Monica's military kitchen breakdown: "Do you want me to cry? Is that what you want? Do you wanna see me cry? Sir, no, sir!"
jokes.setup: Chandler asks how the catering disaster happened
jokes.punchline: Monica's response escalates into a full military drill sergeant breakdown, complete with 'Sir, no, sir!' — she's simultaneously asking for sympathy and running a war room
jokes.explanation: Monica in full control-freak meltdown mode. The 'Sir, no, sir!' is the best element — she's giving herself the drill sergeant order in the middle of an emotional breakdown. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh no! But I already bought my dress!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I mean... that's terrible for you guys.

jokes.text: Monica threatening Ross: 'If you don't help, I'm gonna take those hot dogs and create an appetizer called Pigs In Ross.'
jokes.setup: Ross refuses to help with the wedding catering
jokes.punchline: Monica threatens a very specific, food-themed physical violence — her professional identity and her anger combining into one threat
jokes.explanation: An excellent Monica joke — she threatens Ross with the only vocabulary she has (food). 'Pigs In Ross' is a memorable twist on the food item that's already been established. The character integration is very strong; this threat could only come from Monica in this situation.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Your parents will come around. I'm sure of it. You two are perfect for each other. You're going to have a great marriage.

jokes.text: Ross's assignment: 'Ball a melon!' Chandler's complaint: 'How come I'm stuck dicing when he gets to ball a melon?'
jokes.setup: Monica is assigning kitchen tasks; Ross gets to use the melon baller
jokes.punchline: Chandler's complaint uses 'ball a melon' as a double entendre while also genuinely complaining about an unfair task assignment
jokes.explanation: A functional innuendo gag that works because Chandler is simultaneously genuinely complaining (the task IS more fun) and making an accidental pun. The dual sincerity (both the complaint and the accidental double meaning) is what makes Chandler's innuendo jokes work.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's like I'm Superman, right? But instead of Lois Lane, every woman is kryptonite. I keep flying toward them, thinking 'This is it, this is my moment,' but the second I get close, I'm weakening. My powers disappear. I crash to the ground. And then I have to fly away to some other city to try again.

jokes.text: Monica's first response when Carol announces the wedding may be off: 'You're still gonna pay me, right?'
jokes.setup: Carol announces she and Susan are thinking of calling off the wedding
jokes.punchline: Monica's first thought is about her catering fee — an entirely self-interested response to a human crisis
jokes.explanation: A perfectly Monica response — her financial/professional anxiety overrides her social grace for exactly one beat before she corrects herself. 'Or something a little less selfish' from Rachel immediately after is the button. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, man, I feel completely powerless with women. Like I have no control over the situation.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, I know what you mean. It's like being a remote control with no batteries. You're just sitting there, and nobody wants to use you.

jokes.text: Ross: 'I, uh, can't believe I'm gonna say this, but I think Susan's right.' Carol: 'You do?' Ross: 'Do you love her? And don't be too emphatic about this.'
jokes.setup: Ross is encouraging Carol to go through with the wedding to Susan
jokes.punchline: After asking 'Do you love her?' Ross immediately hedges with 'don't be too emphatic' — his self-interest still peeking through his magnanimity
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ross character joke that carries real emotional complexity. He's trying to do the right thing but can't fully suppress his feelings — 'don't be too emphatic' is the perfect crack in his noble facade. This is sophisticated character comedy: funny AND revealing. High character integration; this is distinctly Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, this is so beautiful. I can feel the spirits here.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: There's an elderly spirit... he's offering me candy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: He says... he says you're going to regret this.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No wait, he's just saying that about all marriages. He's very negative.

jokes.text: Ross to Carol: 'If my parents didn't want me to marry you, no way that would've stopped me.'
jokes.setup: Ross is encouraging Carol to defy her parents and have the wedding
jokes.punchline: He doesn't realize the irony — he's passionately defending his marriage to Carol, the woman who later left him for a woman
jokes.explanation: A nicely layered moment — Ross's declaration of love for his marriage to Carol lands with irony because we know how that turned out. The audience gets a double reaction: the sweet sentiment and the dark humor of its context. Character integration is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, look! Mrs. Adelman's spirit is finally satisfied after seeing this lesbian wedding.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: She's departing peacefully now.

jokes.text: Monica when the wedding is back on: 'You heard the woman! Peel! Chop! Devil! Can't believe I lost two minutes.'
jokes.setup: The wedding is back on and there's still too much to do
jokes.punchline: Monica's immediate return to drill-sergeant mode with 'Can't believe I lost two minutes' as if the emotional moment that saved a relationship was a scheduling inconvenience
jokes.explanation: Excellent Monica character button on the emotional scene. 'Can't believe I lost two minutes' dismisses the entire emotional climax as a scheduling delay — pure Monica. The list 'Peel! Chop! Devil!' is also funny as an incomplete command sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, man, I killed it with the catering today. Those appetizers? Perfection.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You didn't cater anything, did you?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, but I ate like I did. That's basically the same thing.

jokes.text: Joey: 'I feel like Superman without my powers, you know? I have the cape, and yet I cannot fly.' Chandler: 'Well, now you understand how I feel every single day. The world is my lesbian wedding.'
jokes.setup: Joey is lamenting being surrounded by women at a lesbian wedding and unable to flirt successfully — he likens himself to a powerless Superman
jokes.punchline: Chandler appropriates the metaphor to comment on his own chronic inability to be attractive to women, culminating in 'The world is my lesbian wedding'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most quotable exchanges. Joey's Superman metaphor is already good, but Chandler's extension of it — 'The world is my lesbian wedding' — is exceptional. It's a perfectly compressed statement of Chandler's perpetual romantic failure, and the phrase itself is a memorable comic construction. Justifies 8+ clearly.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? You just gotta move on. Find a new woman, start fresh.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Or, you know what? Have a drink.

jokes.text: Chandler: "Well, now you understand how I feel every single day. The world is my lesbian wedding."
jokes.setup: Joey complains about being unable to pursue any women at the lesbian wedding
jokes.punchline: Chandler pivots to his own chronic romantic futility — for him, the whole world might as well be a lesbian wedding
jokes.explanation: The best line in the episode. 'The world is my lesbian wedding' is an extraordinarily efficient expression of Chandler's chronic romantic failure — transforming the episode's central event into a personal metaphor. It requires no explanation, is perfectly Chandler, and is immediately quotable. The economy is near-perfect (six words for the core thought), the character integration is as high as it gets, and it's genuinely original. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor but exceeds it in quotability and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I am having the time of my life! These women are so attentive, so thoughtful... I haven't felt this appreciated since... well, ever! And everyone's being so nice to me, so welcoming. It's like they all want to make sure I'm having a good time. Which, you know, I am!

jokes.text: Mrs. Adelman/Phoebe at the wedding: 'Butterscotch? No one? All right, you'll be sorry later.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe/Mrs. Adelman is attending the wedding ceremony
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Adelman offers butterscotch candies around like a little old lady would at any social event, completely at home despite being a spirit in a stranger's body at a lesbian wedding
jokes.explanation: A perfect character beat for Mrs. Adelman — of course she'd have butterscotch. The mundane detail of offering hard candy at a wedding is funnier than any big joke could be at this moment. 'You'll be sorry later' is a very specific old-lady prediction that lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oy, who needs it?

jokes.text: Mrs. Adelman/Phoebe during the ceremony: 'Oh, my God. Now I've seen everything!' — then the spirit departs
jokes.setup: The minister says 'Nothing makes God happier than when two people, any two people, come together in love' — the ceremony begins
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Adelman, who said she wanted to 'see everything' before she died, finally sees a lesbian wedding and declares completion — then leaves Phoebe's body
jokes.explanation: The best payoff in the episode and one of the best jokes of the episode. The Mrs. Adelman plot has been building all episode toward this: her 'unfinished business' of seeing everything is resolved by witnessing a lesbian wedding. The structure is nearly perfect — the setup was planted 8 minutes earlier and the payoff is both the punchline AND the emotional resolution. 'Now I've seen everything' works on every level. This is professional-grade sitcom structure. Justifies 8+ easily.

jokes.text: Phoebe (back to normal): 'Whoa, she's gone. She's gone. Go ahead, get married. Go, go!'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Adelman's spirit has just departed Phoebe mid-ceremony
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's slightly dazed, relieved instruction to proceed with the wedding — as if she's just gotten off a long phone call and is catching everyone up
jokes.explanation: A functional button on the Mrs. Adelman payoff. 'Go, go!' has a funny urgency to it, like she's ushering traffic. Serves the narrative transition well without being a great joke on its own.

jokes.text: Ross, watching Carol and Susan dance: 'Yeah. Can't help but.' (quietly)
jokes.setup: Monica says 'Would you look at them?' watching Carol and Susan at their wedding
jokes.punchline: Ross's quiet, resigned agreement — 'Can't help but' — contains multitudes: he means he can't help but watch his ex-wife be happy with someone else
jokes.explanation: A small, beautifully economical moment. Three words that function as both comedy (the dryness) and genuine character pathos. Ross has had a full emotional arc this episode and 'can't help but' lands as a perfect, understated closing beat for his story.

jokes.text: Ross to Monica about the pigs-in-blankets: 'How's that pig-in-the-blanket working out for you?' Monica: 'I wrapped those bad boys.'
jokes.setup: At the wedding reception, Ross and Monica are having a quiet moment
jokes.punchline: Ross asks about the pigs-in-blanket with the weight of their whole stressful catering experience behind it; Monica's pride in 'I wrapped those bad boys' is funny given how much drama surrounded it
jokes.explanation: A warm callback to the catering chaos with good character integration. Monica's pride in 'those bad boys' is funny but the joke is relatively low-key. Serves the denouement well.

jokes.text: Joey consoling a woman who misses 'Rose': 'I think it's time you forget about Rose, move on with your life. How about we get you a drink?' She responds warmly: 'Okay. So nice!'
jokes.setup: Joey overhears a woman mourning someone named Rose; he seizes the opportunity to console her
jokes.punchline: His sympathy is entirely predatory — his 'advice' to move on is immediately followed by asking for a drink, revealing he's just using a grieving moment as a pickup line
jokes.explanation: A classic Joey move — weaponizing emotional vulnerability for a pickup. His transition from consolation to invitation is lightning fast and reveals perfect self-interest. 'So nice!' from the woman makes it funnier because his manipulative technique actually works.

jokes.text: Joey, realizing the woman he's trying to pick up is a lesbian: 'I shouldn't even bother coming up with a line, right?'
jokes.setup: Joey has been flirting at a lesbian wedding and realizes his target is not available to him
jokes.punchline: His resigned self-assessment — not outrage or confusion, just pragmatic acceptance that his usual toolkit is useless here
jokes.explanation: A nice payoff to Joey's Superman metaphor earlier. His pragmatic acceptance of defeat — not even defeated, just not bothering — is true to his character. The question form is funnier than a statement would be.

jokes.text: Sandra: 'I just danced with a wonderfully large woman. And three other girls made eyes at me over at the buffet. I'm not saying it's something I wanna pursue, but it's nice to know I have options.'
jokes.setup: Rachel checks in on her mom at the reception
jokes.punchline: Sandra has been hit on by women at the lesbian wedding and — having just announced she's leaving her husband — is open-mindedly noting her options, ending with 'nice to know I have options'
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback that pays off Sandra's storyline with comedy. Given her announcement about leaving Rachel's father, her breezy observation that she 'has options' at a lesbian wedding is nicely darkly comic and character-consistent. 'Wonderfully large woman' is a very Sandra construction.

jokes.text: Ross asking Carol to dance: 'Come on. I'll let you lead.'
jokes.setup: Ross asks Carol to dance at her wedding; she hesitates
jokes.punchline: 'I'll let you lead' — a small, self-aware concession that acknowledges Carol is the one who moved forward in this relationship while he's been catching up
jokes.explanation: A lovely small line. 'I'll let you lead' functions as both a practical dancing instruction AND an emotional acknowledgment of their dynamic. It's funny and touching simultaneously. The economy is excellent — four words doing a lot of work.

jokes.text: One of the women at the wedding: 'Look, penis, schmenis! Okay? We're all people.'
jokes.setup: The wedding is winding down; two women are apparently having some kind of discussion about gender/sexuality
jokes.punchline: 'Penis, schmenis' — the Yiddish dismissal construction applied to anatomy as a way of saying it doesn't matter who has what
jokes.explanation: A sharp, funny piece of background dialogue. The Yiddish dismissive construction ('schmenis') applied to anatomy is genuinely original and funny. High quotability. The character integration is low because it's a guest, but the joke concept itself is good.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'Which one of us is gonna be the first one to get married?' Ross: 'Mon, I was married.' Joey: 'Yeah, me too, technically.' Chandler: 'I had a wedding.'
jokes.setup: Rachel sparks a discussion about who'll get married first
jokes.punchline: Three of the men immediately claim prior marriages/weddings in quick succession — each with escalating qualifications ('I was married' / 'me too, technically' / 'I had a wedding') suggesting varying degrees of non-standard matrimonial experience
jokes.explanation: An excellent closing joke that works on multiple levels. The escalating qualifications ('married' → 'technically' → 'I had a wedding') imply three increasingly dubious matrimonial claims, each funnier than the last. It's a perfect ensemble joke that also serves as a callback to all their backstories. Strong structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Rachel asks 'Which one do you think will be the last to get married?' — everyone immediately looks at Chandler
jokes.setup: After discussing who will be first to marry, Rachel pivots to who will be last
jokes.punchline: The entire group's unspoken, instantaneous consensus (all eyes to Chandler) is the joke — no words needed
jokes.explanation: A perfect visual/reaction joke. The humor is entirely in the group's wordless consensus. The irony (for a rewatcher) that Chandler is the first of the main six to get married makes this an exceptional rewatch joke. Economy is maximal — the joke requires zero dialogue. Strong ensemble character integration.

tmdb_overview: Monica caters the wedding of Ross's ex-wife and her lesbian lover. Phoebe is possessed by the spirit of an 82-year-old massage client who dies in the middle of a session. And Rachel's mom comes to visit and drops a bombshell.
insight: Wedding chaos sustains 56 jokes across 22 minutes without a single standout peak.
